claims.text: PL 117-81 sec. 1683 carries the statutory note '50 USC 3373'; enacted title 'ESTABLISHMENT OF OFFICE, ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, AND AUTHORITIES TO ADDRESS UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL PHENOMENA'; 135 Stat. 2118-2123. Approved 27 December 2021.

Sec. 1683(f) requires a science plan for phenomena 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate any such advanced characteristics and performance.'

Sec. 1683 was wholly replaced by sec. 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Div. F of PL 117-263), which substituted 'SEC. 1683. ESTABLISHMENT OF ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE.' and added the 50 U.S.C. 3373(n) definitions.
Sec. 1683 of P.L. 117-81 is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and required establishment of the office within 180 days of 27 December 2021.

Sec. 6802 of the IAA FY2023 rewrote Sec. 1683 in full, designating the 'All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office' and requiring the Director to report to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI.

Sec. 1683(j) as amended requires a written Historical Record Report within 540 days, drawing on intelligence community records, oral history interviews, interviews of current and former Government officials, and classified and unclassified national archives.

desc: Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, signed 27 December 2021, is the statutory root of the entire modern apparatus. It directed the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to establish within 180 days an office inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense or a joint DoD/ODNI organisation to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. Its enumerated duties reach beyond analysis into governance: synchronising and standardising collection and reporting 'including adverse physiological effects' across DoD and the intelligence community, forcing incident reports into a centralised repository, evaluating links to adversary and non-state actors, and coordinating with the FAA, NASA, DHS, NOAA and the Department of Energy. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, and every subsequent UAP provision — Sec. 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA, Sec. 1687 and Sec. 7343 of the FY2024 NDAA, Sec. 6801 of the IAA FY2025, and Secs. 1671-1673 of the FY2026 NDAA — cross-references it. It was restated in full by Sec. 6802 of the IAA FY2023, which named the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, set the Director reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI, entitled ten named intelligence elements to place detailees inside it, and added subsection (j), the Historical Record Report on the United States Government's dealings with UAP built from intelligence community records, oral histories and interviews of current and former officials.

claims.text: Section 1683 was enacted as Pub. L. 117-81, div. A, title XVI, §1683, on 27 December 2021, at 135 Stat. 2118, and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373.

Pub. L. 117-263 §6802(a) (23 December 2022) amended section 1683 generally, replacing its text, and §1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever appearing, extending the statute's definitional reach to transmedium and submerged objects.

The AARO Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, and reports 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters of the Office.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii) requires the historical record report to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

The same subsection requires itemization of 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

The historical record report must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945, and the Archivist of the United States must make available to AARO NARA holdings 'including classified information' as the Director considers necessary.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e)(1) directs the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(g) requires a science plan to account for characteristics 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.'
Each AARO annual report must include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

The statute defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense, pushing designated materials-testing and medical-study responsibility outward to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories.

Annual reports must name 'the line organizations that have been designated to perform the specific functions under subsections (d) and (e), and the specific functions for which each such line organization has been assigned primary responsibility.'
Subsection (m) required the Secretary of Defense to terminate the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force no later than the date the new office was established.

Public Law 119-60 §1672(b) (18 December 2025) rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to bind 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense'; the prior text reached only IC elements.

connections: AARO and its first Director, Sean Kirkpatrick — the office created by this section; Kirkpatrick reported to the NASA UAP Independent Study Team's 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 events.
Deputy Secretary of Defense and USD(I&S) — the reporting lines written into 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3), which run into the same offices that control the DoD SAP architecture under DoDI 5205.11.

NARA and the Archivist of the United States — obligated by subsection (j)(2) to open classified holdings to AARO; separately the statutory custodian of the UAP Records Collection created by the FY2024 NDAA.

David Grusch — his 2023 allegation of a program 'protected by restricted access' not reported to Congress tracks the exact statutory language of subsection (j)(1)(B)(ii)(I).

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories — Section II.4 demands identification of MITRE work performed for AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP and AAWSAP, connecting the statutory office lineage to contractor custody.

dossier.denialPosture: The statute contains no denial; the office it created does. AARO's Volume I historical record report (8 March 2024) states it found no verifiable evidence that the U.S. government or private industry has ever had access to extraterrestrial technology, and attributes whistleblower accounts to misidentification of authentic classified programs. That formulation concedes the existence of authentic classified programs proximate to the allegations while denying their nature, and it is the denial Chairwoman Luna attacked on the record on 9 September 2025.
dossier.narrative:
Section 1683 began as a modest reorganization and became, through two rewrites, the sharpest disclosure instrument in federal law. Read it as a chronology of what Congress learned.

The original enactment on 27 December 2021 stood up an office to absorb the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, in the wake of the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment. A year later, section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 amended the section generally — replacing it in full — and section 1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever the word appeared. That single-word substitution is not cosmetic. It extended the statute's reach from aircraft to transmedium objects and submerged objects, a definitional move that matters if what is at issue includes things recovered from water.

The rewritten statute names the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office and hardwires a dual chain of command. The Director is appointed by the Secretary of Defense in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with the Secretary. The Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence — and, separately, 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters.' That administrative reporting line runs to the same office that is a SAP Oversight Authority under DoDI 5205.11 and the DoD interface to the DNI's Controlled Access Program Central Office. The office chartered to find concealed compartments is administratively subordinate, in part, to the office that manages compartments.

Subsection (j) is the load-bearing clause. Within 540 days of 23 December 2022, the Director was to deliver to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership a written report on 'the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawn from intelligence community records, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former officials, and classified and unclassified national archives. It must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945. And it must include 'a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.' Subsection (j)(2) obliges the Archivist of the United States to make classified NARA holdings available to the office for that purpose.

Subsections (e) and (g) are where the statute stops sounding like transparency legislation and starts sounding like a program charter. Under (e)(1), the Secretary of Defense in coordination with the DNI 'shall designate one or more line organizations that will be primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Under (e)(2), both officials must issue directives ensuring those line organizations 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Under (g), the science plan must account for performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Congress wrote replication into the law. Subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) then requires each annual report to include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

Definitions matter here too. Subsection (n)(6) defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing materials testing and medical studies out to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories, and therefore out to contractor-operated facilities. Subsection (n)(7) defines transmedium objects as those observed transitioning between space and atmosphere, or atmosphere and water.

The amendment history is the compliance record. In December 2023, P.L. 118-31 §7341 moved the annual report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly onto the AARO Director alone. In December 2025, P.L. 119-60 §1672(b) rewrote subsection (f)(1)(A) so the data-availability mandate binds 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' — the prior text covered only IC elements. Congress had to amend the statute to reach the Department of Defense's own components. Section 1671 added the NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept requirement with a 2004 lookback, and section 1673(a) demanded an accounting of the security classification guides themselves. Each amendment closes a door someone had walked through.
openQuestions: Which line organizations were designated under subsections (d) and (e), and for which functions? The statute requires them to be named in annual reports; no unclassified naming has been published.
Was the science plan required by subsection (g) ever produced, and does it contain a replication program element as the statute contemplates?
Has any annual report actually addressed subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) — efforts 'to capture or exploit' discovered UAP — and what was said?
Did the Archivist open classified NARA holdings to AARO under subsection (j)(2), and what accession records document that transfer?
Why did Congress need to amend subsection (f)(1)(A) in December 2025 to reach DoD components — which components had withheld data under the prior text?

The original 27 December 2021 text of section 1683 differs materially from the 2022 rewrite; what provisions in the original were dropped, and at whose request? The Code preserves only a summary amendment note.
Has the AARO Director delivered the accounting of security classification guides required within 180 days of 18 December 2025, and does it list any guide covering recovered materials?
dossier.whatItIs: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021 at 135 Stat. 2118, is the statute that created the office lineage running from the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force through the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and was rewritten wholesale a year later by section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Public Law 117-263), and amended again in 2023 and 2025.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only place in the United States Code where Congress wrote down, in operative statutory language, that programs concerning unidentified anomalous phenomena may have been 'protected by restricted access' and 'not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' and demanded an accounting of them going back to 1 January 1945. It is also the only statute that directs the Secretary of Defense to designate line organizations for 'the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models' relating to UAP, and to run a science plan whose stated purpose includes providing 'the foundation for potential future investments to replicate' anomalous performance characteristics. Congress did not merely authorize a reporting office; it authorized materials testing, medical study of exposed personnel, and replication research — the exact functional description of a reverse-engineering enterprise — and then required that any prior version of the same enterprise be disclosed. The statute's subsequent amendment history is a record of the Executive branch failing to comply.

Section 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, requires DoD and ODNI to stand up a standing UAP office within 180 days, designate line organizations able to 'rapidly respond to, and conduct field investigations of' UAP incidents, and run a science plan aimed at performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology' and at providing 'the foundation for potential future investments to replicate any such advanced characteristics and performance.'
